content: Seven molecules in human milk could help explain how a mother’s nutrition connects with her baby’s growth, offering a window into the biology of milk production. Human milk contains thousands of nutrients, metabolites, proteins, immune factors, and other molecules, yet researchers have often studied those components one at a time. Much remains unknown about how the gland that produces milk shapes this mixture and how differences in its composition relate to infant growth. By examining those molecules together, a team led by researchers at NYU Grossman School of Medicine identified seven candidate biomarkers associated with maternal nutritional status, infant growth, and biological processes within the mammary gland. Their study, published in Science , analyzed 1,543 milk samples from three geographically and nutritionally diverse cohorts in Canada, Pakistan, and Burkina Faso. The mammary gland prepares for milk production during pregnancy, undergoing hormonal changes that guide cell specialization, tissue and immune remodeling, and metabolic programming. Lactation becomes the main expression of that preparation after delivery. Like the placenta during pregnancy, the gland then serves as an interface between mother and child, connecting maternal biology and nutrition with the developing infant. “Human milk gives us a rare, non-invasive window into the biology of the lactating mammary gland,” said Liat Shenhav, PhD, the study’s senior author and an assistant professor at NYU Grossman School of Medicine, with appointments in the Institute for Systems Genetics, the Department of Microbiology, and the Department of Obstetrics and Gynecology. “By looking at molecular patterns across diverse populations, we can begin to identify shared features of mammary function and understand how maternal nutritional and metabolic state relates to milk composition and infant growth.” The study is one of two complementary papers published in Science from the International Milk Composition (IMiC) Consortium. Conducted in collaboration with Meghan Azad of the University of Manitoba and funded by the Gates Foundation, this international research effort brought together more than 1,000 mother-infant pairs and profiled more than 25,000 molecular features in human milk. For the NYU-led analysis, researchers integrated measurements of metabolites, proteins, micronutrients such as vitamins, macronutrients such as carbohydrates, and human milk oligosaccharides, a group of complex sugars. This approach, called multi-omics, examines several types of molecules together to build a fuller picture of a biological system. The team analyzed these measurements alongside infant growth data using computational tools, including machine learning, a form of artificial intelligence. In two randomized nutritional trials, maternal supplementation promoted recovery or stability in growth among infants at higher risk of poor growth. The molecular analyses also revealed a shared pattern in milk composition associated with both supplementation and infant growth. The companion study examined which milk components could be changed through maternal nutrition. It found that supplementation during lactation increased several B vitamins in milk, while many other components remained comparatively stable. “The studies show that human milk is neither fixed nor simply a reflection of what a mother eats,” said Shenhav. “Some components respond to maternal nutrition, while others remain stable or appear to reflect broader biological states within the mammary gland. Understanding that distinction is essential if we want to design interventions that meaningfully support maternal and infant health.” Mammary cells make and release milk components, while an epithelial barrier regulates what passes between the bloodstream and milk. Tissue remodeling reshapes the milk-producing tissue, and immune and repair processes protect the gland and help it recover from stress or injury. The researchers mapped milk’s molecular patterns onto these interconnected functions. Seven molecules contributed most consistently to the patterns associated with maternal nutritional status and infant growth. Four were short-chain acylcarnitines, called C2, C3, C4, and C5, which help cells process nutrients for energy. The remaining three were the amino acid lysine, the complex sugar 6′ sialyllactose, a human milk oligosaccharide, and the mineral selenium. Together, these candidate biomarkers captured complementary aspects of mammary function, extending beyond established measures of blood-milk barrier permeability, or how readily substances cross that barrier. The acylcarnitines showed the strongest links across the gland’s different functions, particularly C5. Higher C5 levels were associated with molecular signatures of reduced milk synthesis and with patterns related to tissue remodeling and immune activity. C5’s prominence prompted the researchers to examine how maternal nutrition might influence acylcarnitine levels. Acylcarnitine metabolism depends on coenzyme A, or CoA, a molecule central to energy and fat metabolism. The body makes CoA from pantothenic acid, better known as vitamin B5. Drawing on this established biology and associations across the cohorts, the researchers proposed that too little available vitamin B5 may restrict CoA-dependent metabolism and alter acylcarnitine profiles, potentially allowing C5 to accumulate. “Our findings demonstrate the intimate link between maternal nutrition, metabolic health and mammary function, highlighting the importance of an integrative approach to supporting maternal and infant health,” said first author Dr. April Jauhal of the Shenhav lab at NYU Grossman School of Medicine. “One plausible route linking maternal nutrition to mammary metabolism in our data is via the pantothenic-CoA-C5 metabolic pathway, and we are currently investigating the functional role of this pathway in mammary biology and lactation.” The Shenhav Lab is developing a framework that combines computational and experimental work to test potential nutritional bottlenecks that may constrain mammary metabolism and milk production. These include the proposed pathway involving vitamin B5, coenzyme A, and C5. “Ultimately, we want to understand milk in the context of the biology that produces it,” said Shenhav. “The mammary gland sits at a critical interface between maternal physiology and the developing infant. By understanding how maternal metabolism influences mammary function and milk composition, we can begin to uncover the biological pathways linking maternal nutritional status with infant growth.” Milk can be collected repeatedly without invasive procedures, allowing researchers to follow mammary biology over time. The lab is also studying colostrum, the earliest milk, and transitional milk, which precedes mature milk. Researchers want to understand how mammary functional states emerge during the transition from pregnancy to mature lactation, and whether early molecular changes in milk reflect the development of the gland’s metabolic, barrier, and secretory functions. Reference: “Shared patterns of human milk composition link mammary gland function to infant growth” by April Jauhal, Bianca Cordazzo-Vargas, Daniel Sunko, Pratima Niroula, Lishi Deng, Laeticia Celine Toe, Ameer Muhammad, Aneela Pasha, Yasir Shafiq, Naveed Iqbal, Waqasuddin Khan, Andrew Mertens, Kelsey Fehr, Joann M. A brief procedure using saline could offer lasting relief for stubborn carpal tunnel symptoms without steroids, a small clinical trial suggests. The numbness, tingling, weakness, and pain of carpal tunnel syndrome arise when the median nerve, a major nerve running from the forearm, is compressed inside a narrow passage in the wrist. Corticosteroid injections can reduce swelling and ease that pressure, but the relief may be temporary. Associated with repetitive hand and wrist movements, the condition affects roughly 5% to 10% of people over their lifetimes, and its incidence is rising. A randomized trial of 63 patients now suggests that injecting saline around the nerve under ultrasound guidance can provide relief that lasts through six months of follow-up. Adding steroids to the procedure did not significantly improve its long-term benefits. The study was published in Radiology , a journal of the Radiological Society of North America (RSNA) . The procedure, called nerve hydrodissection, uses carefully injected fluid to free the nerve from surrounding adhesions, tissue attachments that can restrict its movement. Ultrasound allows clinicians to guide the injection around the affected nerve. Hydrodissection is generally combined with steroid treatment, so its effectiveness without steroids has remained uncertain. Study lead author Anindita Bose, M.D., assistant professor in the Department of Radiology at Mahatma Gandhi Medical College and Hospital in Jaipur, India, and colleagues studied patients with confirmed carpal tunnel syndrome who had not responded to conventional treatment. “Most of our patients had been suffering from carpal tunnel syndrome for months to years and did not get much relief despite trying various treatments like pain medications, splints, lifestyle modification, and corticosteroids,” said study co-author Anupama Tandon, M.D., professor in the Department of Radiodiagnosis and Imaging at University College of Medical Sciences and Guru Teg Bahadur Hospital in Delhi, India. “It came as a pleasant surprise to find that a simple procedure of dissecting the median nerve under ultrasound guidance with normal saline provided them long-term relief.” To compare the treatments, the researchers randomly divided participants into three equal groups. One received hydrodissection with normal saline, a saltwater solution. Another received hydrodissection with saline and a corticosteroid, while the third received a corticosteroid injection alone. All three treatments were guided by ultrasound. The team tracked symptoms, function, and pain using standardized clinical scores. Ultrasound measurements of the median nerve’s cross-sectional area allowed the researchers to assess changes in swelling. Follow-up assessments took place four, 12, and 24 weeks after treatment. All three groups improved significantly by four weeks, but their outcomes diverged as follow-up continued. “At 12 weeks and 6 months, both hydrodissection groups demonstrated further improvement in clinical symptoms and function, whereas patients who received corticosteroid injection alone experienced a recurrence of the symptoms, suggesting that the initial benefit was short-lived,” Dr. Tandon said. The ultrasound measurements supported the symptom and function results. The median nerve’s cross-sectional area decreased by approximately 43% to 45% after hydrodissection, compared with approximately 15% after steroid injection alone, indicating a greater reduction in nerve swelling. The lack of a significant additional long-term benefit from steroids in the hydrodissection groups matters because those drugs carry risks beyond the possibility that symptoms will return. “Traditional steroid injection for carpal tunnel syndrome often provides only temporary relief, thus requiring repeats of the procedure,” Dr. Tandon said. “Further, steroids carry risk of localized skin changes, fat thinning and tendon weakening.” Hydrodissection took an average of 15 minutes, and patients tolerated it well, with no significant immediate or delayed complications observed. Questionnaire responses indicated high satisfaction with the procedure. It was low-cost, required neither anesthesia nor hospitalization, and allowed patients to return to work within an hour. “Overall, the study suggests that ultrasound-guided saline hydrodissection is a safe, minimally invasive treatment that can provide sustained clinical and morphological improvement in patients with refractory carpal tunnel syndrome,” Dr. Tandon said. “Thus, hydrodissection merits to be a minimally invasive option for mild to moderate carpal tunnel syndrome and can defer and even alleviate the need for surgery.” The researchers said larger studies across multiple centers, with longer follow-up, are needed. They have already launched a study comparing the long-term effectiveness of different fluids used for hydrodissection in carpal tunnel syndrome, including dextrose versus saline. “This trial features an extended follow-up period to track long-term patient outcomes and establish the true durability of the treatment,” Dr. Tandon said. Reference: “Efficacy of US-guided Hydrodissection for Carpal Tunnel Syndrome: A Prospective Randomized Controlled Trial” by Anindita Bose, Anupama Tandon, Gopesh Mehrotra, Siddharth Maheshwari and Ayush Khandelwal, 6 October 2026, Radiology . An antibiotic resistance gene helps a dangerous gut bacterium build tougher spores that can survive hospital disinfectants. A hospital surface can be disinfected and still harbor dormant spores of Clostridioides difficile , a bacterium that causes diarrhea that can be deadly for already sick patients. Researchers have now found that an antibiotic resistance gene can help the bacterium produce tougher spores, allowing them to survive hospital-grade cleaning products and high laundry temperatures. Monash University researchers traced this added resilience to a change in how the bacterium builds its spores. Their study, published in Nature Communications , reveals how acquiring a gene that protects against an antibiotic can also strengthen the form the bacterium uses to spread. C. difficile spores behave much like plant seeds, waiting for suitable conditions to become active again. The human gut provides one such opportunity, making survival outside the body a crucial part of the bacterium’s journey between patients. “Spore survival matters because spores are the main way these pathogens spread between people and through hospitals, homes, and the environment,” said first author Dr. Yogitha Srikhanta, a postdoctoral research fellow at Monash Biomedicine Discovery Institute. Antibiotic resistance is supercharging dangerous gut bacteria to withstand even hospital-grade disinfectants intended to kill them. Credit: Desirel Ng/Monash University The resistance gene produces a protein that takes the place of a key protein used to build spores. With that replacement in place, the bacterium can continue making spores despite an antibiotic that would otherwise block the process. The resulting spores are also tougher, extending the gene’s effects beyond resistance to the drug itself. “Antibiotics are helping bacteria evolve in ways we hadn’t anticipated,” said lead researcher Professor Dena Lyras, director of Monash Biomedicine Discovery Institute and interim dean of Monash’s Sub-Faculty of Biomedical and Psychological Sciences. Bacteria that stop responding to antibiotics can leave infections difficult or impossible to treat. The World Health Organization identifies antimicrobial resistance as a major global health threat and estimates that it contributes to millions of deaths each year. The Monash team describes its study as the first to uncover a link between antibiotic resistance and bacterial spores, connecting treatment resistance with the ability to survive outside a patient. Srikhanta cautioned, “A resistance gene that changes how spores are built could make infections harder to control and help resistant strains spread more easily. “We are now investigating ways to deal with this new type of antibiotic resistance.” Targeting the spores could offer a way to interrupt that spread, although the researchers have yet to establish a solution. Lyras said, “Our new research shows just how sophisticated their evolution is, with the potential to have disastrous impacts on humans. “They are not only better at building tolerance to drugs we develop, but making new versions of themselves that can survive better in particular environments, like surfaces where cleaning products are commonly applied.” Reference: “Uncovering an alternate pathway of antibiotic resistance in spore-forming bacteria” by Yogitha N.
